blocks.text: Ovarian cancer is a malignant tumour arising from the ovary. Some cancers historically labelled ovarian cancer originate in the fallopian tube or peritoneum, particularly high-grade serous carcinoma.
A. Epithelial ovarian cancer
Most common

Includes high-grade serous, low-grade serous, endometrioid, clear cell and mucinous carcinomas. High-grade serous carcinoma is the most common aggressive subtype and frequently arises from the distal fallopian tube.
B. Germ cell tumours
Include dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, immature teratoma and other germ cell tumours. They are more common in adolescents and young women.
C. Sex cord-stromal tumours
Include granulosa cell and Sertoli–Leydig cell tumours. Some produce hormones, causing abnormal uterine bleeding, precocious puberty or virilisation.
OSCE point: In an older woman with persistent abdominal bloating, early satiety, weight loss and an adnexal mass, epithelial ovarian cancer is an important diagnosis to exclude.

Ovarian cancer may present late because early symptoms can be vague and nonspecific.

blocks.text: The Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) combines ultrasound findings, menopausal status and CA-125.
\[ \text{RMI} = U \times M \times \text{CA-125} \]
Here, \(U\) is the ultrasound score and \(M\) is the menopausal score according to the chosen RMI version.

The RMI helps guide referral and investigation; it does not replace clinical judgement. Other systems, such as IOTA ultrasound models and ADNEX, may be used depending on local expertise and protocols.
Histopathology confirms the cancer subtype and informs treatment.

In a patient with a potentially resectable ovarian malignancy, avoid casually performing an unplanned biopsy or cyst aspiration because this may spill tumour cells or compromise definitive surgery. A gynaecological oncology team should determine the appropriate route to tissue diagnosis.
When primary surgery is not appropriate, image-guided biopsy may be used to establish the diagnosis before systemic treatment.

blocks.text: “The scan has shown a mass near the ovary, and some of its features mean that we need to investigate it carefully. This does not, by itself, prove that it is cancer. I would like a specialist team to review the findings and arrange any further tests needed. If cancer is confirmed, the treatment plan will depend on the type of tumour and whether it has spread. I appreciate that this may be worrying, and we will explain each step and support you throughout the process.”

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the most common type of ovarian cancer?
Epithelial ovarian cancer is the most common category. High-grade serous carcinoma is the most common aggressive epithelial subtype.
Q2. What is the classic presentation?
Persistent abdominal bloating or distension, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, and urinary symptoms, sometimes with weight loss or ascites.
Q3. Is CA-125 diagnostic of ovarian cancer?
No. It is a tumour-associated marker that supports risk assessment and may be useful for monitoring selected patients. It can be raised in benign conditions and may be normal in malignancy.
Q4. What ultrasound features are concerning?
Solid areas, papillary projections, irregular thick septations, bilateral complex masses, ascites and other evidence of metastatic disease.
Q5. Why is specialist referral important?
Gynaecological oncologists are experienced in staging, appropriate surgery, cytoreduction and coordinating systemic treatment. Appropriate specialist management can improve the quality of care.
Q6. What is the role of BRCA testing?
It can identify inherited susceptibility, inform family counselling and influence treatment choices, including eligibility for certain targeted therapies.
Q7. Can a woman with ovarian cancer preserve fertility?
Sometimes. This depends on the histological subtype, stage, treatment requirements and individual circumstances. It needs careful specialist counselling.
Q8. What is the difference between primary surgery and neoadjuvant chemotherapy?

Primary surgery aims to remove and stage the disease before chemotherapy. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given first in selected patients, usually followed by reassessment for interval cytoreductive surgery.
Q9. Does a normal CA-125 exclude ovarian cancer?
No. Clinical suspicion and imaging findings still need appropriate assessment.
Q10. Should every ovarian cyst be removed?
No. Many cysts are benign and can be monitored, depending on their size, appearance, symptoms and the patient's menopausal status. Suspicious masses require appropriate specialist assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. How to present your findings in an OSCE

blocks.text: “This is a postmenopausal woman presenting with progressive abdominal distension, early satiety and unintentional weight loss. Examination demonstrates abdominal distension with clinically detectable ascites and a palpable pelvic mass. These findings are concerning for an ovarian malignancy with possible peritoneal involvement.

“My differential diagnoses include ovarian malignancy, a complicated benign adnexal mass and a gastrointestinal primary with secondary ovarian involvement. I would arrange CA-125, pelvic ultrasound and appropriate cross-sectional imaging, assess her general condition and refer urgently to a gynaecological oncology team for definitive evaluation and management.”

Forgetting pregnancy testing in women of reproductive potential.
Performing or recommending unplanned aspiration of a suspicious mass.
Delaying specialist referral while completing nonessential tests.
Discussing treatment without considering histology, stage, fitness and fertility wishes.

blocks.text: Single best answer

A 64-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with progressive abdominal bloating, early satiety and weight loss. Ultrasound shows a complex adnexal mass with solid components and ascites. What is the most appropriate next step?
A. Reassure her because ovarian cysts are usually benign
B. Arrange urgent gynaecological oncology assessment and appropriate staging investigations
C. Repeat ultrasound in one year
D. Aspirate the mass before making a referral

items.text: O — Ongoing abdominal bloating.
V — Vomiting, bowel or urinary symptoms may occur.
A — Ascites or adnexal mass.
R — Risk factors, including BRCA and Lynch syndromes.
I — Investigate with ultrasound, CA-125 and appropriate imaging.
A — Assess through a gynaecological oncology MDT.
N — Need histological confirmation and stage-appropriate treatment.
